<?php
$input = file_get_contents('php://stdin');
$tokens = preg_split('/\s+/', trim($input));
if (count($tokens) < 2) exit;
$n = (int)$tokens[0];
$m = (int)$tokens[1];

if ($n > $m) {
    echo 0;
    exit;
}
if ($n == $m) {
    echo 1;
    exit;
}

$a = array_slice($tokens, 2, $m);
$a = array_map('intval', $a);
sort($a);

$b = [];
$c = 1;
for ($i = 0; $i < $m - 1; $i++) {
    if ($a[$i] == $a[$i + 1]) {
        $c++;
    } else {
        $b[] = $c;
        $c = 1;
    }
}
$b[] = $c;
sort($b);

$x = 0;
for ($i = 1; $i <= 101; $i++) {
    $s = 0;
    foreach ($b as $count) {
        $s += intdiv($count, $i);
    }
    if ($s >= $n) {
        $x = $i;
    }
}
echo $x;
?>

We are given a C program and need to translate it to PHP. Let's analyze the C code first.

The C code:
- Reads n and m.
- If n > m: prints 0.
- Else if n == m: prints 1.
- Else:
   - Reads m integers into array a.
   - Sorts a.
   - Then it compresses consecutive equal elements into counts stored in array b.
   - Sorts b (the counts).
   - Then for i from 1 to 101, it computes s = sum over h of (b[h] / i) (integer division). If s >= n, it sets x = i.
   - Finally prints x.

We need to replicate this logic in PHP.

Important details:
- The C code uses qsort with a comparison function that subtracts integers. In PHP, we can use sort() which sorts ascending.
- The array sizes: a has size m, b has size up to m (but actually r <= m). In PHP we can use dynamic arrays.
- The loop for i from 1 to 101 inclusive. In C, it's `for(i=1; i<=101; i++)`. So i goes 1..101.
- The variable x is updated whenever s >= n, so at the end x will be the largest i (since loop increases i) such that s >= n. Actually the loop goes from 1 to 101, and if condition holds, x = i. So x ends up as the maximum i in 1..101 satisfying sum(b[h]/i) >= n. If none, x remains 0? In C, x is initialized to 0. So if no i satisfies, it prints 0. But note that n <= m (since else if n==m handled, else n<m). And b contains counts of frequencies. The sum of b[h] = m. For i=1, sum(b[h]/1) = m >= n (since n<m). So at least i=1 will satisfy. So x will be at least 1. The loop goes to 101, so x will be the maximum i up to 101 that satisfies. But why 101? Possibly because constraints? In PHP we can just loop 1 to 101.

Edge cases: 
- If n > m: print 0.
- If n == m: print 1.
- Else: compute as above.

We must read from standard input. In PHP, we can use fscanf(STDIN, ...) or read lines.

Let's write PHP code.

Steps:
1. Read first line with n and m.
2. If n > m: echo 0; exit.
3. If n == m: echo 1; exit.
4. Read next line? Actually the C code reads m integers, possibly across multiple lines. In PHP, we can read all remaining integers from STDIN.
   We can read the whole input and split.
5. Store in array a, sort.
6. Compress consecutive equal values into counts array b.
7. Sort b.
8. Loop i from 1 to 101:
   s = 0;
   foreach b as count: s += intdiv(count, i); (integer division)
   if s >= n: x = i;
9. Echo x.

Note: In C, integer division truncates toward zero. In PHP, intdiv does integer division (floor for positive numbers). Since counts are positive, it's fine.

Let's implement.

$tokens = preg_split('/\s+/', trim($input));
Then first two tokens are n and m.
Then next m tokens are the array a.

But careful: The C code reads m integers after n and m. There might be newlines. Using token split works.

Let's code accordingly.

source_data.prob_desc_description: Natasha is planning an expedition to Mars for $$$n$$$ people. One of the important tasks is to provide food for each participant.The warehouse has $$$m$$$ daily food packages. Each package has some food type $$$a_i$$$.Each participant must eat exactly one food package each day. Due to extreme loads, each participant must eat the same food type throughout the expedition. Different participants may eat different (or the same) types of food.Formally, for each participant $$$j$$$ Natasha should select his food type $$$b_j$$$ and each day $$$j$$$-th participant will eat one food package of type $$$b_j$$$. The values $$$b_j$$$ for different participants may be different.What is the maximum possible number of days the expedition can last, following the requirements above?
source_data.prob_desc_output_spec: Print the single integer — the number of days the expedition can last. If it is not possible to plan the expedition for even one day, print 0.
source_data.prob_desc_input_spec: The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$m$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 100$$$, $$$1 \le m \le 100$$$) — the number of the expedition participants and the number of the daily food packages available. The second line contains sequence of integers $$$a_1, a_2, \dots, a_m$$$ ($$$1 \le a_i \le 100$$$), where $$$a_i$$$ is the type of $$$i$$$-th food package.
source_data.prob_desc_notes: NoteIn the first example, Natasha can assign type $$$1$$$ food to the first participant, the same type $$$1$$$ to the second, type $$$5$$$ to the third and type $$$2$$$ to the fourth. In this case, the expedition can last for $$$2$$$ days, since each participant can get two food packages of his food type (there will be used $$$4$$$ packages of type $$$1$$$, two packages of type $$$2$$$ and two packages of type $$$5$$$).In the second example, there are $$$100$$$ participants and only $$$1$$$ food package. In this case, the expedition can't last even $$$1$$$ day.
